stemMd: The passage suggests that the economists described in the third paragraph would be most likely to agree that
instructionsMd: Answer on the basis of the passage only.

options.label: A
options.textMd: queues share the cost of driving among road users more fairly than prices do.

options.label: B
options.textMd: a congestion charge is worth introducing only if its revenue is returned to the drivers who can least afford it.

options.label: C
options.textMd: a congestion charge changes the form in which drivers pay rather than making them pay for something that had been free.

options.label: D
options.textMd: setting the charge at the right level is the single most important decision a city makes.

explanationMd:
The economists' position is compressed into two sentences of the third paragraph, and the inference comes from reading them together.

1. "an untolled road is not free; it is paid for in time" — before the charge, drivers were already paying, in a currency other than money.
2. "A congestion charge converts a queue into a price" — the charge substitutes one currency for the other.

Put those together and the economists' claim is not that a charge imposes a new cost; it is that it changes the **form** of a cost that already existed. That is the claim that a congestion charge changes the form in which drivers pay rather than making them pay for something that had been free.

**Why the passage calls this a "narrower claim".** The paragraph opens by saying these economists "make a narrower claim than either side in that argument". One side said the scheme was fair because the money was recycled; the other said it was unfair because the compensation came late and went to the wrong district. Both are arguments about who ends up better off. The economists decline to take either position, and the passage says so explicitly: "Whether it is handed back well is a political question rather than an economic one." The narrow claim that is left is exactly the change-of-form claim.

**How to check the answer.** For an inference item, test each option by asking whether the passage would have to be rewritten for that option to be false. If the change-of-form claim were false, the sentence "an untolled road is not free; it is paid for in time" would have to go. Now try the same test on the option holding that a charge is worth introducing only if its revenue is returned to the drivers who can least afford it: nothing in the paragraph would need to change, because the paragraph never says a charge is or is not worth introducing.

**Technique.** When a passage attributes a view to a named group, confine yourself to the sentences about that group. The critics' complaints in paragraph two are not the economists' view, and an option that sounds like a reasonable opinion about congestion charging in general is not the same as the opinion the passage assigns.

distractorRationale.b: The passage explicitly refuses this. It says whether the revenue "is handed back well is a political question rather than an economic one", so the economists are described as declining to set any such condition. This option also imports the distributional complaint from paragraph two, which belongs to the critics of the exemption scheme, not to the economists.
distractorRationale.a: This reverses the passage. It says time "is distributed as unequally as money", which makes the queue no fairer than the price, and the following sentence treats the price as the improvement because it "can be handed back" while a queue cannot. The option takes the comparison the passage makes and points it the wrong way.
distractorRationale.d: The final sentence says the opposite: "the design of the exemptions, rather than the level of the charge, is where most schemes succeed or fail". This option picks the term the passage deliberately demotes, which is easy to do if the eye lands on the phrase "the level of the charge" without the words that precede it.

accessibilityText: A question about the accompanying prose passage on Valdera's congestion charge. It asks what the economists described in the third paragraph would be most likely to agree with. There is no figure, table or mathematical notation; the options complete the sentence stem.

provenance.notes: Original item written against the existing original passage bocconi-ug-stim-congestion-charge-006. Two distractors reverse a comparison the passage actually makes and one attributes the critics' position to the economists, so recognition of vocabulary from the passage does not identify the key.

review.author: bocconi-undergraduate-wave4-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: Paragraph 3: an untolled road 'is not free; it is paid for in time' and a charge 'converts a queue into a price' - exactly C. A contradicts 'time is distributed as unequally as money'; B is too strong (they call hand-back a political question, not a precondition); D contradicts 'design of the exemptions, rather than the level of the charge'.

review.notes: Author's uniqueness check: only D is entailed by the pair of sentences about the economists. A is denied by 'a political question rather than an economic one', B is denied by 'time is distributed as unequally as money', and C is denied by the final sentence's explicit ranking of exemption design above charge level. Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key.
